slides.title: A bad release at 11 pm, and no switch to undo it
slides.tldr: Deploying code and opening a feature to users are two separate jobs. A feature flag splits them, so a bad release can be switched off without a deploy.

blocks.title: The switchboard at home
blocks.body: Say a new room has just been wired. If it short-circuits, you don't cut power to the whole neighborhood. You flip that one room's switch to off. Running the wire is the deploy; turning the switch on is the release. Keep the two apart and a mistake means flipping a switch, not pulling out wire.

Ryan's team deploys a new checkout at 11 pm, and it has a bug. Going back to the old code means a rollback deploy, which takes 20 minutes and is risky in itself. For those 20 minutes, customers can't place orders.

blocks.caption: Two ways to fix a bad release

columns.title: Without a flag
items: Rollback deploy: 20 minutes
The rollback can bring new mistakes
Other teams' good changes get rolled back too
columns.tip: The feature and the code are one thing, so undoing the feature means undoing the code.

columns.title: With a flag
items: Switch off: 5 seconds
The code doesn't change, so there is no new risk
Only that feature goes dark; everything else stays on
columns.tip: The code is already deployed and sitting there; only the switch is off. No deploy needed.

blocks.body: Deploy means the code is on the server. Release means users can see it. They are two separate decisions.

aside.body: Open a risky change slowly, and shut it off in a second if it goes wrong, without rolling the code back.

items.meaning: A condition in the code whose on/off state comes from config or data, not from changing the code.
Putting the previous version back in place of the new one.

check.q: Why does a feature flag mean you don't need a deploy to undo a bad checkout?
check.a: The new code is already on the server, just switched off by the flag. If something breaks, you turn the flag off and the old path runs. The code never changes.

slides.title: Four kinds of flags: different jobs, different lifespans
slides.tldr: Flags come in four kinds: release (open a feature slowly), ops/kill switch (emergency off), experiment (A/B) and permission (who gets it). The kind decides the lifespan and the owner.

blocks.body: Not all switches are equal. The main switch of a house stays for years, but the temporary switch for a new room comes out once the work is done. Flags are the same. First decide which kind a flag is, because the kind tells you how long it lives and who is allowed to change it.

blocks.caption: The four kinds of feature flag

rows.tip: A flag to delete as soon as the job is done. This is the kind that piles up the most.

cells: Switching a feature off in an emergency
rows.tip: The switch that lets you turn off a slow payment gateway while the rest of the app keeps running.
Users are split into two groups. Once you see the result, you pick one and remove the flag.
For example, "reports for premium customers". It is really a business rule, not a temporary flag.

blocks.title: The three requirements of a kill switch
items: It can be changed without a deploy (from the database or a config service).
The on-call engineer can find and change it within a minute.
When it is off, the app doesn't crash. It takes a fallback path, such as a "please try again later" message.

marks.tip: The flag is named "off" on purpose: a missing flag defaults to false, so card payments keep working unless someone really pulls the switch.
While the switch is on, customers get a clear message and another way to pay, instead of a hanging page.

items: A kill switch has a price: while it is on, that feature is gone. Build and test the fallback path before the emergency.
For every flag, write down its kind, its owner and when it will be removed. Everything except permission flags and kill switches needs an expiry date.
A permission flag is really an access rule. It belongs under authorization in the security topic.

check.q: The payment gateway suddenly slows down. Which kind of flag lets the on-call engineer shut off that part within a minute?
check.a: An ops flag, or kill switch. It can be changed without a deploy, and while it is off the app runs a fallback path.

slides.title: A simple flag service and percentage rollout in Symfony
slides.tldr: Keep flag state in the database and cache it with a short TTL. For a percentage rollout, hash the user id into 0–99 so the same user always gets the same result.

blocks.body: Don't open a feature to everyone at once; open it in steps. Start at 1% and raise it while everything looks healthy. The key trick: hash the user id together with the flag name and reduce it to a number from 0 to 99. If that number is below the percentage, the feature is on. The same id always gets the same number, so a user who has the feature keeps it.

blocks.caption: Rolling out a new checkout step by step

steps.title: 1. Team only
steps.body: Your own ids on the allow list; percentage 0.
steps.tip: Use it in production yourselves before any real user sees it.

steps.title: 2. 1% of users
steps.body: Compare error rate and order count.
steps.tip: If it goes badly, only 1% are hurt. Turn the flag off and they are back.

steps.body: Run for a day; check that load and errors stay fine.
steps.tip: Problems that only show up under real load come out here.
The flag isn't deleted yet. Keep watching for a few days.

steps.title: 5. Remove the flag and old code
steps.body: Drop the condition and keep only the new path.
steps.tip: Skip this step and flag debt builds up. More on that in a later slide.

marks.tip: A short TTL: when a flag changes in the database, every server knows within 30 seconds at most.
Flag missing, or the database unreachable? The safe default is false: the new feature stays off.
The flag name goes into the hash too, so every flag picks a different 1% of users.

items: Never show a user the feature on and then off. That is why you hash instead of calling random().
Log which flag values each request saw. It is invaluable when you are hunting a bug.
If flag state lives in a config file, changing it needs a deploy, which defeats the whole point.
1% of 300 daily buyers is 3 people, too few to judge by. On a small site, hold each step longer or start at 10%.

check.q: Why does a percentage rollout hash the user id instead of calling random()?
check.a: random() gives a different result on every request, so the same user would see the new path one time and the old path the next. A hash gives the same id the same result every time.

slides.title: Flags in Vue: the server decides, the client displays
slides.tldr: Make the flag decision on the server and send the per-user result to Vue through an API. Vue only shows or hides; enforcement stays on the server.

blocks.body: A Vue app doesn't decide flags itself. The server evaluates every flag for the current user and returns a small JSON object. Vue keeps it in a Pinia store and uses it in `v-if`. But remember that everything in the browser is visible: hiding a button in the UI doesn't make anything safe. The new checkout's API has to be guarded by the same flag on the server (next slide).

marks.tip: Give the client only true/false results. Never expose the percentage or the allow list.
The answer depends on the user, so it is private.

blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useFlagsStore } from '@/stores/flags'
import NewCheckout from '@/components/NewCheckout.vue'
import OldCheckout from '@/components/OldCheckout.vue'

const flags = useFlagsStore()
</script>

<template>
  <NewCheckout v-if="flags.isOn('new-checkout')" />
  <OldCheckout v-else />
</template>

marks.tip: With the feature off, users see the old path. The way back stays intact.

items: Call /api/flags once when the page loads and keep the result in the store. Don't have every component call it separately.
If the flags don't arrive or the request fails, let isOn() return false: the new feature stays off.
If you only hide the button in Vue and leave the API open, anyone can send the request directly and use the closed feature.

check.q: Why isn't hiding a button in Vue enough to protect a feature?
check.a: The browser code and requests are in the user's hands. They can call the API directly. So the server must block it with the same flag.

slides.title: Hiding the button is not a lock: guard the API too
slides.tldr: A hidden button is still a reachable URL. Check the same flag inside the API action and answer 404 while it is off.

blocks.title: The "Staff only" sign
blocks.body: Taking down the "Staff only" sign doesn't lock the back door of a shop. Hiding the button is the sign; the flag check on the server is the lock.

Ryan hides the new checkout's button behind the flag. A curious user opens the browser's network tab, copies the request the new page would send, and sends it by hand. Nothing on the server asks about the flag, so the unfinished checkout runs for a stranger.

marks.tip: The same isOn() call, with the same user, as /api/flags. The hash gives the same answer, so Vue and the server always agree.
404 tells a stranger nothing. A 403 would confirm that a closed feature exists.

blocks.body: The client can hide a feature. Only the server can forbid it.

items: Guard every endpoint the feature owns, not just the first one. One unguarded route is an open door.
If the flag is switched off while a page is open, the next call gets a 404. Let the Vue app reload /api/flags and fall back to the old checkout.

aside.body: Vue decides what to show. The server decides what is allowed.

check.q: A user calls POST /api/checkout/v2 directly while new-checkout is off for them. What should happen, and where is that decided?
check.a: The server answers 404, decided inside the controller action by the same isOn() call. The hidden button in Vue is only decoration.

slides.title: Flag debt: the switch nobody flips
slides.tldr: Old release flags that were never deleted keep two code paths alive, double your tests and create places people are afraid to touch. Give every flag an owner and a removal date.

blocks.body: If a switchboard has year-old switches that nobody recognizes, nobody dares to touch them. Code is the same. 10 flags means 1,024 possible combinations in theory, yet only a couple are ever tested. The saddest case: someone flips an old flag by mistake, and its old path broke long ago.

blocks.code:
new-checkout:
  type: release
  owner: 'ryan'
  created: '2026-11-01'
  remove_by: '2026-12-15'      # the CI test below fails after this date
payments-kill-switch:
  type: ops
  owner: 'oncall-payments'
  runbook: 'wiki/payments-kill-switch'

marks.tip: Every release flag gets a removal date. Once it passes, CI or a weekly report speaks up.
An ops flag carries a runbook: what happens when you turn it off, and when to use it.
Ops flags have no remove_by, so only release flags are checked against today.
On the due date the build turns red and names the flag. Nobody has to remember.

blocks.title: Rules for removing flags
items: Once the feature is at 100%, remove the flag and the old path within a week.
If the feature is canceled, remove the flag and the new path, and keep the old one.
Create a ticket and treat the cleanup as part of the release, not as "I'll do it later".

blocks.body: A flag whose job is done is now debt. Removing it is part of finishing the feature.

use: Release and experiment flags: remove them when the work is done.
avoid: Nesting one flag inside another. It tangles the logic.

items: A red build on the due date is the point. If the date truly can't be met, move remove_by in a reviewed commit; never skip the test.

aside.body: Every flag is born carrying its own date of death.

check.q: A release flag has sat at 100% in the code for two months. What harm can it do?
check.a: You have to keep two code paths alive, you need twice the tests, and if someone flips the flag by mistake the old, broken path switches back on.

slides.title: It works on my machine, but not in prod
slides.tldr: Addresses, passwords and settings hardcoded in the code are right in one environment and wrong in another, and a password that reaches git is leaked for good. Keep config outside the code.

blocks.title: The wedding kitchen's recipe and ingredient amounts
blocks.body: The recipe is the same: lasagna. But the ingredient quantities for 50 guests and for 500 guests are different. If you wrote the quantities inside the recipe, you would have to reprint the recipe every time. So the recipe stays fixed and the quantities go on a separate slip of paper. The code is the recipe; the config is that slip.

Ryan wrote the database address and the payment gateway key straight into the code. On staging he found the code writing to the production database! A few weeks later an intern pushed the code to public GitHub, payment key included.

blocks.caption: Config inside the code vs config outside it

columns.title: Inside the code
items: Database address written in the code
A separate build for every environment
Passwords live in git history forever
columns.tip: Changing config means changing code, and secrets travel into git along with it.

columns.title: Outside the code
items: The address comes from an environment variable
One build for every environment
Secrets live in a separate, safe place
columns.tip: The code is the same everywhere and the values arrive at run time. Secrets never enter the repository.

blocks.code:
-    private const DB_URL = 'mysql://root:secret@prod-db.internal/shop';
+    #[Autowire(env: 'DATABASE_URL')] private string $dbUrl,

 # staging server:     DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:...@staging-db.internal/shop
 # production server:  DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:...@prod-db.internal/shop

marks.tip: The host and password are baked into the code, and into every git copy of it. Staging runs this same line, so it would write to the production database.
The code only names the variable. Its value is supplied from outside when the app starts.
Each server holds its own value and the code is identical everywhere, so staging can no longer reach the production database by mistake.

blocks.body: Whatever changes between environments belongs outside the code.

aside.title: The key sitting on GitHub
aside.body: Within hours of a payment key landing in a public repository, automated scanners find it. Deleting the key afterwards doesn't help, because it stays in git history. The only fix is to rotate it: issue a new key.

items.meaning: Where the app runs: dev (your own machine), staging (a dress rehearsal), prod (the real thing).
Settings that change from one environment to another. They are kept outside the code.

check.q: What goes wrong between staging and prod if you hardcode the database address?
check.a: You have to change the code for every environment, and one slip makes staging write to the production database. Keep the code the same and supply the address from outside, and that mistake can't happen.

slides.title: Build once, run everywhere
slides.tldr: The 12-factor rule: the same build or image runs in every environment, and the differences come from environment variables. What you tested on staging is exactly what ships to prod.

blocks.title: One pot cooked, served differently
blocks.body: The cook makes a single pot. If one table wants it spicier, the chilli goes in a separate bowl; nobody cooks the dish again. A built image is that pot, and the env variables are the bowl of chilli.

blocks.caption: One image, two environments, different env variables

nodes.label: CI build
nodes.tip: Builds one image after the tests pass. No environment ever gets a build of its own.

nodes.label: Image v42
nodes.tip: No passwords or addresses inside. Every environment gets this same image.

nodes.label: Staging
nodes.tip: Runs with its own database and its own payment sandbox key.

nodes.label: Production
nodes.tip: The real database and the real key, supplied from outside at run time.

edges.label: CI builds the image from the code, once
It runs on staging with the staging env variables
On prod it is the same image, with only prod's env and secrets

blocks.title: What you gain
items: What you tested on staging is exactly what runs on prod, with no risk from a separate build.
Changing config doesn't need a new build: change the env and restart.
There are no secrets in the image, so nothing is lost if someone gets hold of it.

blocks.body: Build the code once. Decide its behavior at run time, with environment variables.

items: One catch: a Vue app built with Vite bakes its `VITE_` values into the files at build time. For one build everywhere, load a small `config.json` when the app starts.

aside.body: "It was fine on staging, but broke on prod" often means the two places were actually running different code or different builds.

check.q: What risk do you create by making a separate build for every environment?
check.a: The build you tested on staging isn't the one that runs on prod, and separate builds can contain different code. With one image, exactly what you tested is what runs.

slides.title: Using env variables in Symfony
slides.tldr: Put safe defaults in .env and the real values on the server. In code, inject them with types via #[Autowire(env: 'int:NAME')], and in YAML write %env(int:NAME)%.

blocks.body: Symfony reads the `.env` file, but real environment variables on the server always win. `.env` goes into git and holds only safe defaults. Changes for your own machine go in `.env.local`, which stays out of git. Env variables are always strings, so when you need a number or a true/false, add a processor (`int:`, `bool:`). In YAML the same thing reads `timeout: '%env(int:PAYMENT_TIMEOUT)%'`.

blocks.code:
APP_ENV=dev
PAYMENT_TIMEOUT=5
SEARCH_ENABLED=1
PAYMENT_BASE_URL=https://sandbox.pay.example
# PAYMENT_API_KEY is not here: it is secret, so it lives in the secrets vault

marks.tip: It looks like a number, but it is a string. You need int: to turn it into a number when it enters the code.
Even the name of a secret doesn't have to be written here. The next slide shows where it goes.
The int: processor turns the value into a number as it is read. Passing the string "5" as a timeout would be wrong.
The bool: processor turns "1", "true", "on" and similar values into true.
No address or number is written in the code. It all came from outside.

aside.title: Where does each value come from?

items.desc: Which value comes from which .env file
Which env variables the app uses

items: APP_ENV is for Symfony itself to read. Don't write if (APP_ENV === 'prod') in your own code. See the pitfall slide.
In production, `composer dump-env prod` compiles .env into a PHP file, so nothing is parsed on every request.

check.q: Why do you need the int: processor to inject PAYMENT_TIMEOUT=5 as a timeout?
check.a: Because env variables are always strings. The int: processor turns the value into a number. Without it, the string "5" arrives and you get a type error or odd behavior.

slides.title: Config and secrets are not the same thing
slides.tldr: Leaking an address or a timeout does little harm; leaking a password or an API key does. Keep secret values in the Symfony secrets vault or a secret manager, never in git.

blocks.title: The restaurant's ingredient list and the safe key
blocks.body: If the sheet of ingredient quantities leaks, little is lost. If the key to the safe leaks, the restaurant gets emptied. So the sheet hangs on the wall while the key stays on the owner's belt. That is why you keep config and secrets apart.

rows.tip: Harmless if leaked, and a new developer can run the app straight away.

cells: Server env or the deploy tool
rows.tip: Outside the code, and specific to each environment.

cells: API key, DB password, JWT private key
Secrets vault or cloud secret manager
rows.tip: Encrypted or stored separately, and never in the repository as plain text.
Check once that it is listed in .gitignore.

blocks.code:
# the "quick" way
PAYMENT_API_KEY=sk_live_4f9c0a7e21b8d3

marks.tip: Now the live key sits in git history and in every clone. Deleting this line later removes it from the file, not from the history.
A secret is read like any other env variable, so the code doesn't change. Where the value lives (vault, server, .env.local) is decided outside.

blocks.body: A secret never goes into git. If one gets there by mistake, don't just delete it: rotate the key.

items: The vault's encrypted files and the encrypt key go into git. The prod decrypt key must not (the dev one may): give prod the SYMFONY_DECRYPTION_SECRET variable.
Larger systems use a cloud secret manager or HashiCorp Vault. These also give you value rotation and audit trails.

check.q: Of a timeout and a payment API key, which can sit in .env in git, and which can't?
check.a: The timeout can, because leaking it does no harm. The API key can't; it belongs in the secrets vault or a secret manager.

slides.title: When environments drift apart: config drift
slides.tldr: If code changes behavior by checking APP_ENV, or environments slowly move apart, then tests on staging no longer show how prod behaves. Put the differences in config, not in code branches.

blocks.body: Two kitchens use the same recipe, but one cook quietly adds more sugar. After a few months the two dishes taste different. That is **config drift**. The most common cause is writing `if (prod)` inside the code. Then prod's path never runs on staging, and it runs for the first time right in front of the customer. The cure is one code path everywhere, where only the values change.

marks.tip: The path that sends the real SMS runs only on prod. Nobody has tested it on staging.
Staging and prod run different code paths, so a staging test is no guarantee for prod.

blocks.code:
services:
    App\Sms\SmsGateway: '@App\Sms\BulkSmsGateway'
    App\Sms\BulkSmsGateway:
        arguments:
            $baseUrl: '%env(SMS_BASE_URL)%'   # staging: sandbox URL, prod: the real one

when@dev:
    services:
        App\Sms\SmsGateway: '@App\Sms\LogSmsGateway'

marks.tip: The code always calls the SmsGateway interface, with no new if. Config decides which implementation it gets.
Staging and prod run the very same sending code. Only the address differs: staging points at the SMS provider's sandbox, so nobody gets a real text.
In dev, a log replaces the real SMS. The difference sits in one place where you can see it.

blocks.title: Four ways to stop drift
items: Give staging the same database version, the same image and the same list of env variables as prod.
Change config through code review or the deploy tool, never by hand on a server.
Fail fast on a missing env variable: Symfony throws `EnvNotFoundException` when a service first needs it, so run a smoke request after every deploy.
Regularly compare the env variable names on staging and prod.
Don't read APP_ENV in your own code to change behavior. Let Symfony do that for you (when@dev, per-environment config).
Logging into a server and editing .env.local by hand is the most common source of drift.

aside.body: No if (prod) in the code. Keep the differences in config.

check.q: If code changes behavior with if (APP_ENV === 'prod'), why does a passing staging test not guarantee prod?
check.a: Because the prod branch never runs on staging, so you tested a different code path. If the difference lives in config, the same code path runs everywhere.

slides.title: Discount rules that change every week
slides.tldr: When the business team changes a rule once a week, waiting for a developer and a deploy each time is slow and irritating. That raises the question of moving such rules into data.

blocks.title: The parking garage rate chart
blocks.body: A parking garage cashier knows the procedure for collecting fees: read the entry time on the ticket, find the hours on the chart, read the fee, take the money. When rates go up, the garage posts a new chart, and nobody has to retrain the cashier. The procedure is the code; the chart is the data. The only question is whether your rule is a chart or a procedure.

At Ryan's e-commerce company, the marketing team changes the discount rules every week: "10% off the first order", "free delivery above $50". Every change means a ticket, code, a review and a deploy. Changing one small number takes three days, and the developers are fed up.

blocks.caption: How long a discount change takes to go live (minutes)

items.label: Rule in code
items.tip: Ticket, code change, review, test, deploy: a wait at every step.

items.label: Rule in data
items.tip: The business person changes it in an admin screen. But it brings its own risks, covered in the next slides.

blocks.body: Move a rule into data and it no longer passes through code review. You have to build the safety net yourself.

aside.body: A rule that changes often, and is changed by people who aren't developers, shouldn't wait for a deploy every time.

items.meaning: A business decision that ends up in code: who gets how much discount, which orders must be held back.
A setup that keeps rules outside the code as data and evaluates them at run time.

check.q: What do you save by moving rules into data, and what extra responsibility do you take on?
check.a: You save the wait for a developer and a deploy. But you lose the safety of code review, tests and versioning, so you have to build those yourself.

slides.title: Should a rule live in code or in data?
slides.tldr: Decide with four questions: how often it changes, who changes it, what a mistake costs, and how complex it is. Simple, frequently changed rules with a capped downside go in data; complex or risky ones stay in code.

blocks.body: The rate chart is data, but the rule "a fee is never negative" is part of the procedure. Ask four questions about every rule. The more answers that point towards data, the safer it is to move the rule out of the code. And if you do, testing, versioning and audit become your job; the next slides show how.

rows.tip: For a rarely changed rule, the effort of moving it into data never pays off.
If developers make the changes anyway, code is easier, with review and tests as a bonus.

cells: Limited, or capped by a limit in code
rows.tip: If a mistake is expensive, keep the rule in code, or at least put a hard ceiling in code.
Put a complex rule into data and the data slowly turns into a poor programming language.

blocks.body: In code: risk, complexity and hard limits. In data: numbers, lists and simple conditions that change often.

use: A discount percentage, which cities get delivery, the amount above which delivery is free.
avoid: Tax calculation, balance updates, legal obligations. A mistake in these does direct damage.

aside.body: The chart goes in data; the procedure stays in code.

check.q: Which is the better candidate for data: the tax calculation rule or "10% off the first order"? Why?
check.a: The discount rule. It changes often, it is simple, and a mistake costs little. A mistake in tax calculation carries legal risk, so that stays in code.

slides.title: Running rules with Symfony ExpressionLanguage
slides.tldr: Store each rule's condition as a string in the database and let ExpressionLanguage evaluate it. Pass only a small facts DTO, and check each rule with lint() when you save it.

blocks.body: Imagine each discount is one database row: a condition (`cart.total >= 5000 and user.firstOrder`), a percentage and a priority. The code just loops over the rows and applies the discount of the first condition that matches. Symfony's ExpressionLanguage runs that condition string in a safe, limited language. But remember that the condition is really code, so limit who may write it, and pass a small facts object rather than an entity.

marks.tip: Give the rule only the facts it needs: numbers and flags. Hand it a Doctrine entity and the rule can know and call far too much.
The condition string runs here. The first rule that matches decides the discount.
Whatever is written in the data, the code will never give more than 30% off. The hard limit stays in code.
Lint before saving. Only the names cart and user are recognized; any other name is caught immediately.

items: Don't parse the string on every request. Give ExpressionLanguage a cache pool (a constructor argument) so the parsed result is kept.
Keep the group of people who can change rules small, and log every change.
Money in rules is whole cents (100 cents = $1), so 5000 means $50. Never store money as a float.
Never run user input (for example, text a customer typed) as an expression. Only trusted staff may write them.

items.meaning: A plain object that only carries a few values and does no work of its own.
Checking that a text is written correctly without running it.

check.q: Why pass a small CartFacts DTO instead of the entity?
check.a: The rule sees only what it needs and can't call the entity's other methods. And when the entity's shape changes, the rules stored in the database don't break.

slides.title: Versioning, testing and dry-running rules
slides.tldr: Rules kept in data must go through versioning, tests and approval, just like code: a new version, tests, a dry run on old orders, a start date, and the old versions kept.

blocks.body: Moving rules into data doesn't reduce your responsibility. You now have to build what code review gave you for free. Fixing a rule isn't just editing a row; it means writing a new version, so that later you can answer "which rule gave order 1023 its discount?".

blocks.caption: A safe path for changing a rule

steps.title: 1. Write a new version
steps.body: Don't edit the old row; add a new one called v4.
steps.tip: The old version stays, so you can roll back and you can audit.

steps.title: 2. Run the tests
steps.body: Example-based tests: which cart should get what discount.
steps.tip: You can check the rule is written correctly without any deploy.

steps.title: 3. Dry run
steps.body: Run it over the last 30 days of orders and see what discounts would have been given.
steps.tip: This catches a rule that suddenly gives everyone a discount.

steps.title: 4. Approval
steps.tip: What review is to code, this is to rules.

steps.title: 5. Go live on a date
steps.body: Use valid_from to start at a set time.
steps.tip: At midnight everything switches by itself, with no hand on a switch.

steps.title: 6. Record the version on the order
steps.body: Note which discount came from which version.
steps.tip: When a question comes up about an order, you can say exactly which rule applied.

marks.tip: One test, many cases. Include values on both sides of every boundary: $50.00 and $49.99.
Dropping the exact boundary (≥) is the most common mistake, and this is where the test catches it.
Replay real past orders: what the old rules gave, against what the new rules would have given.
Cents times percent points, divided by 10,000, gives dollars. Say it prints 412 orders changed and $18,300 more: a typo is now visible before anyone sees it.

items: In bigger systems, a cousin of the dry run is shadow mode: run the new rule for real, but only log what it would do, without applying it.
Keep a change log of who changed which rule, when, what changed and who approved it.

check.q: What do you gain by creating a new version instead of editing the old rule's row?
check.a: The version recorded on the order tells you exactly which rule gave the discount, and if something goes wrong you can go back to the earlier version.

slides.title: The price of getting rules-as-data wrong
slides.tldr: Unguarded rules can turn a single typo into a 100% discount, and complex rules in data become an untested programming language. Keep the ceiling in code.

blocks.body: A change in code passes through review and tests. A number on an admin page goes straight to production without any of that. Here is a realistic incident: someone in marketing meant to type "10" and typed "100".

blocks.caption: One typo, direct damage from the admin screen

actors.label: Marketing
actors.tip: A business person who doesn't read code and only uses the admin form.

actors.label: Rules table
actors.tip: The rules stored as data. No tests, no approval.

actors.label: Checkout
actors.tip: Reads the rule on every order and applies the discount.

actors.label: Customers
actors.tip: News of the discount spreads and hundreds of buyers arrive.

messages.note: Live at once, nobody saw it

messages.tip: Hundreds of orders in an hour. Every one of them is legally valid.

marks.tip: Whatever the data says, the code's limit holds. A typo's damage stops at 30%.
When the cap is exceeded, log it and raise an alert. You can fix the admin screen later, but before the damage is done.

blocks.title: Safeguards for rules in data
items: Hard limits (maximum discount) live in code. Raising one needs a deploy; that is the price, on purpose.
Validate when saving: lint the condition and reject a percent above the cap.
Keep only small rules in data; complex branching, loops and state stay in code.

blocks.body: Move rules into data and the risk goes with them. Keep the limits in code, and require a separate approval for changes.

items: The inner-platform effect: the rule language gradually gains loops, variables and functions, and a weak programming language grows inside your database, with no debugger and no tests.
No developer fully understands the rules any more. Nobody owns them.

aside.body: The numbers go in data; the limits stay in code.

items.label: Build vs buy: building or buying a rules engine

check.q: Someone types a 100% discount by mistake on the admin page. What must exist, and where, so the damage never exceeds 30%?
check.a: A ceiling in code, such as min($percent, 30). Whatever is written in the data, the code never goes past the cap, and logs it when it is exceeded.
